blocks.markdown: A **contract of insurance** is an agreement whereby one undertakes for a consideration to indemnify another against loss, damage or liability arising from an unknown or contingent event. One party (the insurer) promises protection against a possible or uncertain event in exchange for consideration, usually a premium.

A person may insure their own life or their child's life without needing spousal consent. Unless the policy says otherwise, rights in a policy on someone's life or health pass to that insured person when the original policy owner dies.
Elements of a contract of insurance

sourceRefs.section: i. Elements of a contract of insurance

blocks.markdown: The commonly taught elements are: **(1)** a subject matter in which the insured has an insurable interest; **(2)** a risk or peril insured against, involving an unknown or contingent event; **(3)** the insurer's undertaking to indemnify or pay benefits if the covered event occurs; **(4)** consideration, usually the premium paid or agreed to be paid, subject to the statutory rules on when a policy becomes binding; **(5)** a meeting of minds between the parties on the essential terms of the insurance agreement.

sourceRefs.section: i. Elements of a contract of insurance

blocks.markdown: **Trap: Section 51 is not the elements list.** The syllabus associates “Elements” with Section 51, but the actual text of Section 51 lists what the written policy must specify: parties, amount, premium, property or life insured, the insured's interest (if not absolute owner), covered risks, and duration. These required policy contents are very important, but they are not the same list as the doctrinal elements above. The fuller treatment of Section 51 as required policy contents is in the policy lesson; the same statutory text is also quoted there (INS1 paras 39-40; INS2 paras 25-27).

sourceRefs.section: i. Elements of a contract of insurance
i. Elements of a contract of insurance

blocks.markdown: **Consensual in formation:** formed through the parties' agreement, but the Code's premium-payment rules determine when the policy becomes valid and binding in the cases covered by Section 77. **Aleatory:** the value each party gives or receives depends on an uncertain event. **Personal:** the risk, representations, and circumstances of the insured matter, and transfer of insured property does not automatically transfer the policy. **Utmost good faith:** both sides must deal honestly and disclose material facts as required by insurance law. **Contract of indemnity:** property recovery generally compensates the actual insured loss, while life insurance ordinarily pays the sum fixed by the policy (Section 186). **Conditional:** the insurer's obligation depends on the policy's conditions, risks, exclusions, and claim requirements. **Often a contract of adhesion:** the insurer normally drafts the standard policy, and ambiguous provisions may be construed against the drafter when legal rules permit, as discussed in Philamcare.

sourceRefs.section: Case digest: Philamcare Health Systems, Inc. v. Court of Appeals

blocks.markdown: **Exam cue.** Do not automatically assume an HMO/health-care agreement falls outside insurance law because it is called a “health-care agreement.” Analyze the actual promise and the risk assumed.

sourceRefs.section: Case digest: Philamcare Health Systems, Inc. v. Court of Appeals

blocks.markdown: The Code looks at what a business actually does, not just its name or whether it earns a profit. A business may be conducting insurance activity if it assumes insurance risk or performs the statutory equivalents, including arrangements designed to evade regulation.
